Personal financial literacy belongs on the required curriculum of secondary schools because young people are entering adulthood with a demonstrable knowledge gap that carries real economic consequences. Surveys of young adults consistently reveal high rates of credit card debt, minimum-payment cycles, low emergency savings, delinquency on student loans, and susceptibility to predatory lending products, and these patterns track closely with the absence of any formal instruction in budgeting, interest, credit, and taxation. States and districts that have introduced mandatory personal finance coursework have reported measurable improvements in credit scores and reductions in high-cost borrowing among the graduates who received it. The correlation cuts in the intuitive direction: when young people are asked to make consequential decisions about compounding interest, loan terms, and long-term saving without ever having encountered those concepts in a structured setting, many of them make choices they later regret, and the financial vulnerability that follows shapes years of their adult lives. Requiring the subject in school is a direct response to a documented harm.

Beyond the question of harm, financial literacy has a claim to curricular space that few electives can match, because it is genuinely universal in a way that most subjects are not. Every graduate, regardless of whether they enter the trades, enlist, attend college, start a business, or move directly into the workforce, will pay taxes, sign a lease or mortgage, encounter credit, save for retirement, buy insurance, and weigh major purchases against income. A student who becomes a plumber needs to understand cash flow and self-employment taxes; a student who becomes a physician needs to understand loan amortization and investment vehicles; a student who inherits nothing and one who inherits substantially both benefit from understanding how to preserve and grow what they have. Unlike subjects whose relevance depends on a particular career path, personal finance applies with equal force across income levels, family circumstances, and vocations, which makes it an unusually efficient use of instructional time.

Finally, secondary schools occupy a position no other institution can replicate: they are the last stage at which society has reliable, structured, near-universal access to young people before those people begin making financial decisions with lasting consequences. Families vary enormously in their capacity and willingness to teach these skills, and the students whose households cannot provide that instruction are precisely the ones most exposed to the costs of not having it, which means leaving the subject to the home reproduces inequality rather than addressing it. Banks, employers, and government agencies interact with young adults only after the first consequential choices have already been made, usually about student debt, credit cards, or a first paycheck. Schools reach students during the narrow window in which prevention is still possible, and that logistical fact, combined with the documented consequences of the current gap and the universality of the skill itself, is what makes a required course the appropriate policy response.
--- END ---
